traveler: Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani (Abdul Qadir Gilani), Ghawth al-A'zam
title: The Gate That Took His Name: Gilan to Bab al-Sheikh, and the Order Built on a Grave
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Na'if, birth on the first of Ramadan
stops.date_confidence: The day is attested as 1 Ramadan 470 AH. Reference sources give the Common Era equivalent as 1077 or 1078 and fix no month, so the year is defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In a village called Na'if, in the district of Rezvanshahr on the southwestern shore of the Caspian, a son is born to Abu Salih and Umm al-Khayr Fatima on the first day of Ramadan. The Talysh mountains stand behind the house; in front of it lie the rice fields, the rain, and the flat grey water. The district is Gilan, and the boy will carry its name across the whole of Islam: al-Jilani, the man from Gilan. A rival tradition puts the birth at a place called Jil inside Iraq instead. Historians set that aside in favour of the name itself.
suggested_refs: The Rezvanshahr district of Gilan on the Caspian coast, traditional site of the village of Na'if
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rezvanshahr, Gilan' (for the coordinates, which correct two wrong points carried in the research pool)

stops.name: Na'if, the infant who will not drink by day
stops.date_confidence: Undated devotional tradition, placed here at the first Ramadan of his infancy. No primary hagiography could be fetched this session: sunnah.org and masud.co.uk both returned 404.
stops.campa: The story the order tells about his first year is this. Through the daylight hours of Ramadan the infant refuses his mother's milk and takes it only after sunset, keeping a fast no one has asked of him and no law requires of a child. The village reads it the way villages read such things, and the reading travels: here is an ascetic who began before he could speak. Qadiriyya devotional literature repeats it for eight centuries. No text earlier than the hagiographers of the fourteenth century could be reached to say who told it first.
suggested_refs: al-Tadifi, Qala'id al-Jawahir, and al-Shattanawfi, Bahjat al-Asrar, the two hagiographies that carry the childhood legends
sources: Widely repeated in Qadiriyya tariqa literature; primary text not accessed this session

stops.name: Gilan, the house without a father
stops.date_confidence: Undated. Tradition places the father's death in the boy's childhood and gives no year; the date here is a placement inside that window, not a claim.
stops.campa: Abu Salih dies while the boy is small, and the household passes to Umm al-Khayr Fatima and, in some accounts, to a maternal grandfather of Sufi lineage. Both families will later be claimed as channels of descent from the Prophet, through Hasan on one side and Husayn on the other, which is how a provincial boy from a wet green province acquires, in retrospect, the blood of a sharif. Modern scholars split on whether the lineage is genuine or was built for him afterward by men who needed him to have it.
suggested_refs: The sayyid genealogy prefixed to Futuh al-Ghaib in his son's hand, tracing the line back through Ali ibn Abi Talib
sources: General Qadiriyya biographical tradition, not independently verified this session

stops.name: Gilan, the road out at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: The departure and the year 1095 are attested in standard reference biography. The forty dinars and the vow are hagiography and carry no date.
stops.campa: At about eighteen he leaves the Caspian for Baghdad, which is where a serious boy goes to read law. Tradition adds the departure scene the order has never let go of: his mother sews forty gold dinars into the lining of his coat against the road, and makes him promise that whatever happens he will speak the truth. She is sending him nine hundred kilometres over the Zagros passes into the capital of Sunni learning, and the only equipment she insists on is a vow. The vow gets tested before the coat is out of Persia.
suggested_refs: The medieval caravan road from Gilan through the Zagros to Iraq
sources: Standard Qadiriyya hagiography for the coins and the vow

stops.name: Near Hamadan, the truth told to the bandits
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The robbery is hagiography; no source fixes where on the road it happened. Hamadan sits on the standard medieval route from Gilan to Iraq and is used as the conventional site. The bandit chief is unnamed in the standard tellings.
stops.campa: The caravan is taken on the road. A robber asks the boy whether he is carrying anything, and the boy says yes, forty dinars, sewn into the lining here. The men laugh, then check, then stop laughing. Brought before their chief and asked why he gave up money nobody would have found, he answers that his mother made him promise to tell the truth and he is not going to break it for gold. The chief, in every telling, abandons the trade on the spot. Later tellers gave him a name; the name belongs to a saint born thirty years after al-Jilani died, and is dropped here.
suggested_refs: The Hamadan stage of the Gilan to Baghdad road, conventional site of the robbery story
sources: Standard element of Qadiriyya hagiography; location traditional and disputed, not confirmed against a primary text this session

stops.name: Baghdad, the cup filled to the brim
stops.date_confidence: Legendary and undated. Wikipedia's Qadiriyya article presents the cup and the rose as a founding narrative of the order, not as an event.
stops.campa: He comes into the greatest city in Islam as one more provincial student with a Persian accent. The legend of his arrival says a shaykh of the city sends him a cup filled so full that a drop more would spill it: Baghdad already has all the holy men it can hold, go home. Al-Jilani sets a rose on top of the water and sends the cup back unspilled. Whether or not anyone did this, the order that later took his name kept the rose, and the rose is still on its banners eight hundred years later.
suggested_refs: The rose emblem of the Qadiriyya, traced by the order to the cup legend
sources: Wikipedia, 'Qadiriyya' (given there as legendary founding narrative)

stops.name: Baghdad, the school of Abu Sa'id al-Mukharrimi
stops.date_confidence: The pupillage and the Bab al-Azaj siting are attested; no source dates the years of study.
stops.campa: He reads Hanbali jurisprudence under Abu Sa'id al-Mubarak al-Mukharrimi, whose small school stands by the Bab al-Azaj gate on the east bank. Some sources give the teacher's name as al-Makhzumi, which is a different nisba and not a variant spelling: one points at a Baghdad quarter, the other at a clan of Quraysh. The distinction is left standing. What matters for the next seventy years is the address. He teaches at this gate for the rest of his life and dies in the schoolroom. The district around it is renamed after him later.
suggested_refs: The Bab al-Azaj quarter of east Baghdad, later renamed Bab al-Sheikh

stops.name: Baghdad, the circles of Ibn Aqil and Ja'far al-Sarraj
stops.date_confidence: Undated. Both pupillages are attested; no source gives years, and no building or quarter is named for either.
stops.campa: He studies Hanbali theology with Abu al-Wafa Ibn Aqil, the sharpest and most quarrelled-with mind in the school, forced more than once to recant in public for reading philosophy. He studies the transmission of hadith with Abu Muhammad Ja'far al-Sarraj. This is the ordinary apparatus of a Baghdad legal education and it takes years, and the sources that record the names record nothing else: not where the sessions were held, not how long they ran, not what the student was like in them.
suggested_refs: The Hanbali teaching circles of eleventh-century Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the seller of date syrup
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The mentorship is attested in standard reference biography with no year and no named place.
stops.campa: The turn from law to the path comes through Abu'l-Khayr Hammad ibn Muslim al-Dabbas, whose trade is in dibs, the thick date syrup sold in the Baghdad markets. He is a hard teacher and by every account a rough one, and the jurist submits to him. Nothing in the record explains why a promising Hanbali lawyer put himself under a tradesman. The order that came afterward has a ready explanation for it. That explanation was written by men with a stake in the answer, and the reason stays a gap.
suggested_refs: The date-syrup markets of twelfth-century Baghdad, trade of Hammad al-Dabbas

stops.name: Baghdad, the ground near Bab Khurasan
stops.date_confidence: A placement, not an event, set at the late end of the student years so the segment reads in order. No source records al-Jilani going to this ground. The pin is the one the atlas already carries for the execution of al-Hallaj.
stops.campa: The city he is reading law in is also a graveyard of the path he is about to enter. Near Bab Khurasan, a hundred and seventy years before he arrives, al-Hallaj was flogged, mutilated, crucified and burned for a sentence. Junayd, who had tested and released Hallaj as a young man and who taught the sober Baghdad Sufism al-Jilani's own chain will run back through, lies at the Shunuziyya cemetery across the water. Ibrahim ibn Adham, the prince who walked away from Balkh, has a disputed grave here too. The student walks past all of it daily.
suggested_refs: The execution ground near Bab Khurasan and the Shunuziyya cemetery, today Sheikh Ma'ruf

stops.name: Iraq, twenty-five years without a place name
stops.date_confidence: Undated and unlocated. Tradition gives roughly twenty-five years of retreat in the deserts and ruins of Iraq and no site survives in any reachable source. The pin is Baghdad because Baghdad is the only fixed point; this is stated as a gap rather than filled with invented places.
stops.campa: After his studies he goes out into the deserts and the ruins and stays there, by the count later biographers give, about twenty-five years. He eats what is thrown away, sleeps in abandoned buildings, speaks to almost nobody. This is a quarter of a century of a documented man's life with not one place name attached to it, not one date, not one witness who says he saw him. The order fills the gap with wonders. The reachable record supplies none of them, and this file keeps the quarter century empty.
suggested_refs: The ruined Sasanian and early Abbasid country around Baghdad, setting of the retreat in the hagiographies
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abdul Qadir Gilani' (duration and general character only; no sites given)

stops.name: Baghdad, the chair of his dead teacher
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1119 in Wikipedia's 'Qadiriyya' article. It sits in direct tension with the 1127 date the same encyclopaedia gives for his return to public preaching; the tension is carried in the next stop and not resolved.
stops.campa: Abu Sa'id al-Mukharrimi dies, and the school by the Bab al-Azaj gate passes to his student. It is a small institution and nobody records how many were in it. The name Qadiriyya is not attached to the building yet and will not be for generations; it is still his teacher's madrasa, and he is a man in his forties who has spent most of his adult life outside the city eating refuse. The building he takes charge of in this year is the building his tomb will be under.
suggested_refs: The madrasa of Abu Sa'id al-Mukharrimi at Bab al-Azaj, nucleus of the later Madrasa al-Qadiriyya

stops.name: Baghdad, the eight years nobody accounts for
stops.date_confidence: This stop is the contradiction itself. One Wikipedia article dates his succession to the school to 1119; another dates his return to open preaching to 1127. Either he held the school quietly for eight years or one of the dates is imprecise. Printed, not adjudicated.
stops.campa: Two reference articles about the same man give two dates that will not sit together. In one he takes over the madrasa in 1119. In the other he does not come back to public life until 1127. Between them lie eight years in which the head of a Baghdad school apparently teaches nobody the sources thought worth naming. Either the headship was quiet and small, or one of the two dates is wrong. Nothing reachable this session decides it, and the eight years stand here as a hole in the middle of the biography.
suggested_refs: The two conflicting datings of the succession and the return to preaching

stops.name: Baghdad, the night he dreams of Iblis
stops.date_confidence: The single precisely dated event of the retreat window. The twenty-first discourse of Futuh al-Ghaib is headed with the night of Sunday, 12 Dhu'l-Hijja, AH 516, which falls in early 1123; the day of the Common Era month is approximated.
stops.campa: One of his discourses carries a date at the head of it, which almost nothing else in his life does: the night of Sunday, the twelfth of Dhu'l-Hijja, in the year five hundred and sixteen. He is in a crowd, in a dream, and he has Iblis in his hands and is about to kill him, and Iblis asks him what the charge is. The discourse that follows is the answer. In a life reconstructed almost entirely from other men's memories, this is one of the few hours he timed himself.
stops.quote: I saw Iblis in a dream, where I was in the midst of a big crowd. I was on the point of killing him, when he said to me (may Allah curse him): "Why are you going to kill me? What is my offense?"
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, Twenty-first Discourse (On addressing Iblis the accursed), trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: The twenty-first discourse of Futuh al-Ghaib, dated in its own heading to 12 Dhu'l-Hijja AH 516
sources: Futuh al-Ghaib, trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing

stops.name: Baghdad, the chair on the open ground
stops.date_confidence: The 1127 return to public preaching is attested. The detail of a chair set up outside the gate because no room would hold the crowd is traditional narrative, not confirmed to a primary text this session.
stops.campa: At about fifty he starts speaking in public and does not stop for thirty-nine years. The tradition says the first sessions are held on the waste ground outside the gate, on a chair carried out for him, because no room in the school will take the number of people who come. He preaches in Arabic that reference works describe as plain to the point of bluntness, to porters and jurists in the same audience. Baghdad has had famous preachers before. It has not had one the city walks out of its own walls to hear.
stops.quote: Three things inevitably demand the attention of every believer under all circumstances: A commandment to be obeyed, a prohibition to be respected, and a divine decree to be accepted with good grace.
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, First Discourse, trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: The open ground outside the Bab al-Azaj gate, traditional site of the first public sessions
sources: Standard tariqa hagiography for the outdoor preaching

stops.name: Baghdad, the school enlarged
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The expansion is attested without a year. The name Madrasa al-Qadiriyya is retrospective, attached after his death by the order named for him, and is not what the building was called while he taught in it.
stops.campa: The building he inherited is torn down and rebuilt bigger, with lodging for the students who come from Persia, Syria, Egypt and further out, and a hall that will hold the numbers standing in the road. Reference works call the result the Madrasa al-Qadiriyya, which is a name from later: in his lifetime it is his teacher's school with his own crowd in it. He lives inside it. He will still be living inside it thirty-six years from now, on the day he dies, and the students will bury him in its floor.
suggested_refs: The Madrasa al-Qadiriyya at Bab al-Azaj, rebuilt on the site of al-Mukharrimi's school

stops.name: Baghdad, mornings of tafsir, afternoons of discipline
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The teaching pattern is attested without any year attached.
stops.campa: The day at the madrasa is cut in two. Mornings he teaches hadith and the exegesis of the Quran, the work of a Hanbali jurist with a licence to instruct. Afternoons he teaches the discipline of the self, which is the other thing, and which men in Baghdad had been executed for teaching within living memory of his own teachers. He does both in the same building on the same day and offers no defence of the pairing. After him the law and the path stop being two hostile addresses in the same city.
stops.quote: There is Allah, and there is your own self, and you must address the situation. The self is the opponent and enemy of Allah.
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, Tenth Discourse (On the self and its states), trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: The divided teaching day at the Madrasa al-Qadiriyya, morning tafsir and afternoon spiritual discipline

stops.name: Baghdad, the birth of Abd al-Razzaq
stops.date_confidence: The year 1134 is attested for the son's birth; no month or day is given.
stops.campa: A son is born to him and named Abd al-Razzaq. He will grow up in the madrasa, become his father's disciple, take the chair after him, and write down in his own hand the genealogy that opens the collected discourses, tracing the line back through Ali ibn Abi Talib. He will also be credited, in some listings, with a book his father is credited with elsewhere. The order's memory of the father is going to pass through this son's hands, which is the reason the memory is difficult to check.
stops.quote: These are the words of my father (may Allah, Exalted is He, bestow His approval upon him!), Supporter of the Imams, Master of the Orders, Abu Muhammad Muhyi'd-din 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani al-Hasani al-Husaini al-Siddiqi, son of Abu Salih Musa Jangi Dost...
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, Author's Genealogy, recorded by his son Shaikh 'Abd al-Razzaq, trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: The Author's Genealogy prefacing Futuh al-Ghaib, in Abd al-Razzaq's hand

stops.name: Baghdad, the household and the crowd
stops.date_confidence: Undated, and the figures are unverified. Tradition gives four wives and a family variously counted at forty-nine children, twenty-seven of them sons, and hundreds of conversions after his sermons. None of these numbers could be cross-checked against a primary genealogical or chronicle text this session.
stops.campa: Around the teaching there is a household the size of a small quarter: four wives, and children the tradition counts at forty-nine, twenty-seven of them sons, several of whom become scholars. Shaykh Qadib al-Ban is among the disciples whose names later transmission chains keep. Jews and Christians are said to have converted in the hundreds after hearing him, and rulers of the age, Nur al-Din Zangi among them, are said to have sought his blessing. Every one of those numbers comes from men who wanted them large.
suggested_refs: Qadiriyya transmission chains naming Shaykh Qadib al-Ban among his disciples
sources: Widely repeated in Qadiriyya biographical tradition; numeric details not independently verified
Wikipedia, 'Abdul Qadir Gilani' (for Qadib al-Ban and the Zangi connection)

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Ghunya li-Talibi Tariq al-Haqq
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The attribution is stable across reference listings; no source dates the composition, and no critical edition was consulted this session.
stops.campa: He writes, or dictates, a manual for men who mean to walk the road: al-Ghunya li-Talibi Tariq al-Haqq, Sufficient Provision for Seekers of the Path of Truth. It is a book of Hanbali law and a book of devotional practice bound as one thing, ablutions and prayer times and inheritance shares in the same volume as the discipline of the heart. Muhtar Holland's English rendering is the title that stands. A version circulating as Treasure for Seekers is not a recognised translation of this book and is dropped.
suggested_refs: Muhtar Holland's translation, Sufficient Provision for Seekers of the Path of Truth, Al-Baz Publishing, 1995
sources: Open Library (Holland's translation and its standard title)

stops.name: Baghdad, the discourses gathered as Futuh al-Ghaib
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The discourses were spoken over years and collected afterward; only the twenty-first carries an internal date. Composition dating not checked against a critical edition.
stops.campa: The sermons are taken down as he gives them and gathered into Futuh al-Ghaib, Revelations of the Unseen: seventy-eight discourses on poverty, on being tested, on the enemy inside a man. The register is not consoling. He tells the seekers that when they have cut themselves off from creatures they must stop asking people for anything with their tongues, and then stop asking in their hearts, because the inward request is the same request. The book will still be printed in Lahore and Houston eight hundred years later.
stops.quote: Once you have isolated yourselves from creatures to devote yourselves to the Truth, do not ask people for anything with your tongues, and when you have given that up, do not ask them for anything in your hearts, for asking inwardly is just like asking in words.
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, Fifteenth Discourse (On fear and hope), trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: Futuh al-Ghaib in the Holland (Al-Baz) and Aftab-ud-Din Ahmad (Sh. Muhammad Ashraf, Lahore) translations
sources: Futuh al-Ghaib, trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Fath al-Rabbani and a disputed title
stops.date_confidence: Undated, and one attribution is unsettled. Al-Fath al-Rabbani is listed under his name without dispute. Jila' al-Khatir is listed under his name in one Wikipedia article and under his son Abd al-Razzaq's name, as Jala-ul-Khawatir, in another. The usual scholarly reading is that these are the father's sermons compiled by the son. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: A second collection of sermons is gathered as al-Fath al-Rabbani, the Sublime Revelation. A third book, Jila' al-Khatir, the polishing of the heart, is harder to hand to anybody with confidence: one reference article gives it to him, another gives the same title to his son Abd al-Razzaq. The likeliest account is that these are the father's words written down by the son, which is also the account that makes it impossible to say where the father stops and the son begins. The conflict is printed rather than settled.
stops.quote: Do not exert yourself to attract prosperity or to avert misfortune. Prosperity will come to you if it is your lot, whether you seek to acquire it or view it with distaste.
stops.quote_source: Futuh al-Ghaib, Thirteenth Discourse (On submission to Allah's command), trans. Muhtar Holland, Al-Baz Publishing
suggested_refs: The conflicting attributions of Jila' al-Khatir between al-Jilani and Abd al-Razzaq Gilani

stops.name: Baghdad, Sirr al-Asrar and the other book of that name
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The attribution of Kitab Sirr al-Asrar wa Mazhar al-Anwar to al-Jilani is stable in reference listings. The title collision noted in this stop is flagged as a bibliographic hazard, not as a claim about him.
stops.campa: He writes Kitab Sirr al-Asrar wa Mazhar al-Anwar, the Secret of Secrets. Another Arabic book carries almost the same name and nothing else in common: the pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-Asrar, an invented letter from Aristotle to Alexander, which Europe will read for four centuries as the Secretum Secretorum in Latin, Hebrew, Spanish and, by 1528, English. Two unrelated books, one title, both in circulation in the same language at the same time. No source consulted separates them for the unwary cataloguer.
suggested_refs: The pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum Secretorum, an unrelated Arabic Sirr al-Asrar, traced in aristotle.journey.json

stops.name: The Tigris at Baghdad, the boat that does not founder
stops.date_confidence: Undated karamat. No source names a landmark or a bank, and the point given is an approximate position on the channel through central Baghdad, corrected from a pooled coordinate that fell two and a half kilometres inland.
stops.campa: On the river the stories multiply. A boat going down under its load is steadied; in other tellings he crosses the water on foot in front of men who came to watch him fail. The Tigris karamat is one of the fixed set the order carries, and no version of it names a bank, a bridge, or a year. Baghdad has been telling wonder stories about its holy men since Hallaj was walked to the gallows through these same streets, and it does not stop for al-Jilani.
suggested_refs: The Tigris channel through central Baghdad, between the Jumhuriya and Jadriya crossings
sources: Standard Qadiriyya karamat narrative; not independently verified, primary hagiographic texts inaccessible this session

stops.name: Mecca, the pilgrim who is also in Baghdad
stops.date_confidence: Undated, and internally contradictory. The best-known version holds he was seen performing the Hajj rites at Mecca while physically preaching in Baghdad; a less common strand insists on an actual physical pilgrimage. The two strands contradict each other and neither is resolved in any source reachable this session.
stops.campa: There is no journey to Mecca in his documented life, and the tradition supplies one anyway: pilgrims swear they saw him at the rites while the congregation at Bab al-Azaj swears he never left the chair. A quieter strand of the same tradition says he simply went. Abu Yazid al-Bistami circled this stone three centuries earlier; Ibn Battuta will circle it two centuries later and ride on to Baghdad; the boy Abdelkader will circle it in 1825 and go looking for this grave. The stone is the atlas hinge, and al-Jilani may or may not have touched it.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, contested in the karamat of the two places
sources: Standard Qadiriyya karamat narrative, contradictory strands noted

stops.name: Baghdad, the foot on the neck
stops.date_confidence: Undated tradition, and verified absent from his own writings: the full texts of both English translations of Futuh al-Ghaib were searched this session for the phrases foot is on, neck of every, and necks of every, with zero hits in either. The saying belongs to the Ghawth al-A'zam legend, not to the discourses.
stops.campa: The sentence the whole later order stands on is the one he did not write down. My foot is on the neck of every saint: a claim of precedence over every friend of God alive, and the ground of the title Ghawth al-A'zam, the Supreme Helper. Abu Madyan in the Maghreb is said to have heard it in spirit and bowed to it. Schimmel traces the words to Jami's Nafahat al-uns. They are in none of the seventy-eight discourses, in either translation, searched line by line.
stops.quote: My foot is on the neck of every saint
stops.quote_source: Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam, p. 247, citing Jami, Nafahat al-uns, p. 527; a hagiographic tradition, not a text al-Jilani wrote
suggested_refs: Jami, Nafahat al-uns, p. 527, earliest chain reachable for the qadam saying
sources: Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam, ch. 5, p. 247
Futuh al-Ghaib, Holland and Aftab-ud-Din Ahmad translations, searched in full: negative result

stops.name: Baghdad, death at the madrasa
stops.date_confidence: The day is attested as 11 Rabi' al-Thani 561 AH and the Common Era year as 1166. No reachable source states a Common Era month; a lens of the research pool gave May, which does not correspond to the AH date, and is not carried. Defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He dies on the eleventh of Rabi' al-Thani in the year five hundred and sixty-one, in the school he has lived in for thirty-nine years. He is about ninety-one lunar years old, which is eighty-eight or eighty-nine by the sun. The date will outlast almost everything else about him: eight centuries on, Sufi communities from Konya to Kano still keep the eleventh of that month as Gyarvi Sharif, the Eleventh, and know whose day it is without being told.
suggested_refs: The Madrasa al-Qadiriyya at Bab al-Azaj, where he lived from 1127 until his death

stops.name: Bab al-Azaj, the gate takes his name
stops.date_confidence: Attested burial at his own madrasa at Bab al-Azaj. The coordinates are the mausoleum's own, and are byte-identical to the pin abdelkader.journey.json already uses for this shrine; a third figure carried in the research pool was 1.7 km off and is discarded.
stops.campa: They bury him in the floor of his own school, and the quarter around it stops being called Bab al-Azaj. It becomes Bab al-Sheikh, the Sheikh's Gate, and it is still called that. Every element of what will be the Qadiriyya order is now in place except the order: a grave, a lineage, a body of sermons, a district named for a dead man. The tariqa will be assembled around this stone over the next two centuries by descendants who were not born when he was buried.
suggested_refs: The Bab al-Sheikh quarter of Baghdad, named for the grave at its centre

stops.name: Baghdad, the son in his father's chair
stops.date_confidence: The succession of Abd al-Razzaq is attested. The claim that he wrote the hagiography which established his father's reputation is downgraded: the only support is one unreferenced sentence, and the dedicated article on Abd al-Razzaq records no such work.
stops.campa: Abd al-Razzaq takes the chair, holds the madrasa until his own death in 1207, and sets down the genealogy that opens his father's discourses. Reference prose credits him with the hagiography that made his father famous across Islam. The hagiographies that actually did that come much later and from other men, and the honest position is that the son kept the school and the papers and the name, which was enough. What he did not do was invent the cult; the cult had time.
suggested_refs: Abd al-Razzaq al-Jilani, shaykh of the madrasa from 1166 to 1207
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abdul Razzaq Gilani' (which records no hagiography by him)

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn Arabi's twelve days
stops.date_confidence: The 1205 visit is attested in ibn_arabi.journey.json. That the Andalusian visited al-Jilani's tomb specifically is not attested anywhere reachable; the sources name Junayd and Hallaj, and the omission is left as an omission.
stops.campa: Thirty-nine years after the burial, Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi comes through Baghdad from Andalusia and stays twelve days, paying his respects to the scholars of the city and its shrines. The tombs the sources name him at are Junayd's and Hallaj's. Bab al-Sheikh is a short walk from either of them, and no source says he went. Two men who both carried the title Muhyi al-Din, Reviver of Religion, in one city inside four decades, and the record puts no meeting and no visit between them.
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's Baghdad stay of 1205 and the shrines named in it

stops.name: Baghdad, the boy from Balkh at the old graves
stops.date_confidence: Attested in baha_ud_din_walad.journey.json and cross-carried in junayd_al_baghdadi.journey.json. Whether the family also visited al-Jilani's shrine is not recorded.
stops.campa: Baha ud-Din Walad comes down the road from Balkh ahead of the Mongols with his household and his young son Jalal al-Din, and stops in Baghdad to pray at the graves of the old masters, Junayd and Ma'ruf al-Karkhi. The boy will be Rumi. The circuit of tombs his father walks him through is by now the standard one, and al-Jilani's, fifty-three years old and already drawing pilgrims, has been absorbed into it. Behind them the army that will take this city in thirty-nine years is still moving west.
suggested_refs: The Baghdad tomb circuit of the early thirteenth century

stops.name: Baghdad, the caliphate ends and the order does not
stops.date_confidence: The Mongol sack of Baghdad is attested to February 1258. That the Qadiriyya continued as a functioning institution through it is attested in Wikipedia's 'Qadiriyya' article without detail on how.
stops.campa: Hulagu's army breaks the walls, kills the last Abbasid caliph, and empties the libraries into the river. The five-hundred-year capital of Sunni Islam stops being a capital in a fortnight. The school at Bab al-Sheikh keeps going. A grave and a chain of teachers turn out to be harder to destroy than a caliphate. The network that will later be called the Qadiriyya loses its city and keeps its succession, and passes through the worst year in Baghdad's history still transmitting.
suggested_refs: The Mongol sack of Baghdad, February 1258, and the survival of the Qadiriyya through it

stops.name: Baghdad, the hagiographers arrive late
stops.date_confidence: Al-Shattanawfi died 713 AH / 1314 CE and al-Tadifi 963 AH / 1556 CE; the stop is pinned to the earlier death. Neither Bahjat al-Asrar nor Qala'id al-Jawahir could be reached in translation this session, which is the single largest gap in this file.
stops.campa: A hundred and fifty years after the burial, al-Shattanawfi writes Bahjat al-Asrar, and two and a half centuries after that al-Tadifi writes Qala'id al-Jawahir, and between them they make the al-Jilani the Islamic world remembers: the infant who fasted, the boy who told the truth to bandits, the man in two places at once, the foot on the neck. Almost every colourful thing in this file comes from these two books. Neither could be read this session. The wonders are reported at second hand, and they are marked as such.
suggested_refs: al-Shattanawfi, Bahjat al-Asrar; al-Tadifi, Qala'id al-Jawahir
sources: Named in the research pool as the foundational hagiographies; neither text reachable this session

stops.name: Baghdad, the bridge of boats
stops.date_confidence: Attested in ibn_battuta.journey.json for the 1320s Baghdad crossing.
stops.campa: Ibn Battuta crosses the pontoon bridge on the Tigris, a road of lashed boats, on an itinerary that by now treats visits to the tombs as a fixed obligation of the traveller rather than an option. The city is a Mongol provincial town with a Persian governor and no caliph. The shrine culture is what survived, and al-Jilani's grave has been part of it for a hundred and sixty years: not a curiosity on the route but one of the reasons to take the route at all.
suggested_refs: The Baghdad bridge of boats described in the Rihla

segments.name: The Order That Took His Name

stops.name: Bab al-Sheikh, the chains that leave the tomb
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim: by the end of the fifteenth century the Qadiriyya had distinct sub-orders and had spread to Morocco, Spain, Turkey, India, Ethiopia, Somalia, and present-day Mali. The stop is dated to the close of that century, not to any single event.
stops.campa: By the end of the fifteenth century the sub-orders have gone out from this grave to Morocco, Spain, Turkey, India, Ethiopia, Somalia, and the western Sahel of present-day Mali, each transmitted teacher to teacher through generations of his descendants. Reference works call him the founder of all this. He founded no tariqa and gave no initiation to any of it; he taught in one building for thirty-nine years and was buried in it. The order is the work of the men who came after and needed a grave to stand on.
suggested_refs: The fifteenth-century sub-orders of the Qadiriyya and their transmission chains

stops.name: Baghdad, the shrine thrown down
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The Safavid capture of Baghdad in 1508 under Shah Ismail I is followed by the destruction of Sunni religious sites, and Ismail I's own article names al-Jilani's tomb explicitly among them.
stops.campa: Shah Ismail I takes Baghdad for the Safavids and goes through the Sunni shrines of the city one by one. Al-Jilani's is named explicitly in the list of what is pulled down. Three hundred and forty-two years after the burial, the grave that had outlasted the Mongols does not outlast a change of confession, and the quarter that carries his name is left holding the name and no building. It stays that way for twenty-seven years, which in the history of a shrine is a season.
suggested_refs: The Safavid capture of Baghdad, 1508, and the destruction of the Sunni shrines

stops.name: Baghdad, the dome of Suleiman
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1535, one year after the Ottoman capture of Baghdad in 1534 and the year the eyalet was established. What the mausoleum record specifies for 1535 is a dome raised over the shrine, not a wholesale rebuilding of shrine and mosque; the research pool's stronger wording is not carried.
stops.campa: The Ottomans take Baghdad back in 1534, and the following year Suleiman the Magnificent has a dome raised over the grave. It is still standing today, which makes it the oldest thing in this file that can be walked into. A Sunni sultan in Istanbul spends imperial money on the tomb of a Persian-born Hanbali preacher in a frontier province he has held for one year, which is the clearest measure available of what the name had become by then: not a local saint, but an asset a caliph-claiming empire wanted its flag over.
suggested_refs: The dome raised over the shrine by Suleiman the Magnificent in 1535, still standing

stops.name: Harar, the shrines of the Qadiri Harari
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The Qadiri Harari suborder and its shrine network in and around Harar and at Borama in Somaliland are attested; no source reachable this session dates the foundation, and the year here is a placement inside the Horn's Qadiri centuries.
stops.campa: In the walled city of Harar and out across to Borama in the Somali country, the Qadiri Harari keep a network of subsidiary shrines, each one a local tomb wired back through a chain of named teachers to the grave at Bab al-Sheikh. This is how the order actually travels: not as a book but as a graveyard, one saint at a time, each new tomb claiming the old one as its root. The Horn of Africa acquires a Baghdad genealogy without anyone from Baghdad ever coming.
suggested_refs: The Qadiri Harari shrine network of Harar and Borama

stops.name: Linxia, the tomb of Qi Jingyi
stops.date_confidence: Khwaja Abdullah is reported to have entered China in 1674 and preached until his death in 1689; his student Qi Jingyi Hilal al-Din (1656-1719) rooted Qadiri Sufism there and is buried at Linxia, which became the Chinese centre. The stop is dated to Qi Jingyi's death; the research pool had compressed the sequence so that Linxia appeared to derive from Khwaja Abdullah.
stops.campa: A preacher named Khwaja Abdullah enters China in 1674 and walks the country teaching until he dies in 1689. It is his student Qi Jingyi, called Hilal al-Din, who puts the Qadiriyya into Chinese ground, and it is Qi Jingyi's grave at Linxia, the Da Gongbei, that becomes the order's centre in China. Six and a half thousand kilometres from Bab al-Sheikh, the same mechanism runs again: a tomb, a chain of teachers, a name from Baghdad nobody there has seen.
suggested_refs: The Da Gongbei shrine of Qi Jingyi at Linxia, centre of the Qadiriyya in China

stops.name: El Guetna, a son named for the Baghdad saint
stops.date_confidence: Attested in abdelkader.journey.json and in Wikipedia's article on Abdelkader El Djezairi. The father's office as muqaddam of the Qadiriyya zawiya of Oued El-Hammam is attested.
stops.campa: Six hundred and forty-two years after the burial, in a hamlet on the Wadi al-Hammam near Mascara, Sidi Muhyi al-Din al-Hasani, shaykh of the Qadiriyya and marabout of the Hachem, names his newborn son Abd al-Qadir. The name is already common in the family tree. The zawiya the boy is born into is a Qadiriyya house, school and court and refuge at once, running on a chain of transmission that its members trace teacher by teacher back to one madrasa by one gate in Baghdad.
suggested_refs: The Qadiriyya zawiya of Oued El-Hammam near Mascara, headed by Sidi Muhyi al-Din al-Hasani

stops.name: Mecca, the hajj of the seventeen-year-old
stops.date_confidence: The 1825 departure on hajj is documented. The month is traditional, carried from abdelkader.journey.json, which marks it as such.
stops.campa: At seventeen the boy sets out with his father on a journey that will run more than two years and carry him through Tunis, Cairo, Mecca, Medina, Baghdad and Damascus. He circles the Kaaba at his father's side, in the same crowd out of Fez and Delhi and Istanbul that Abu Yazid al-Bistami circled it in nine centuries earlier and Ibn Battuta five centuries after that. The pilgrimage is not over at Mecca. The Qadiriyya have a second address, and it is east, in Iraq.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, station of the 1825 hajj

stops.name: Bab al-Sheikh, the Algerian at the tomb
stops.date_confidence: Only the 1825 departure on hajj is documented; no reachable source dates the Baghdad leg. The research pool's own lenses split, one giving 1825 and two giving 1826, one of those to February. The 1826 year is carried for continuity with abdelkader.journey.json, which marks it traditional, and the month is dropped.
stops.campa: The pilgrimage bends east, and a boy from Algeria kneels at this grave and renews in his own person the chain his father heads two thousand miles west. He is named for the man under the stone. He does not yet know that he will spend seventeen years at war with France, five in French prisons, and one July morning in Damascus standing between a mob and thousands of Christians because his law told him to. The order gave him the name; the tomb is where he comes to sign for it.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani at Bab al-Sheikh, Baghdad

stops.name: Damascus, the other tomb of the same pilgrimage
stops.date_confidence: Traditional, carried from abdelkader.journey.json. This stop also corrects a geographic error in the research pool, which read the source as placing the graves of both Ibn Arabi and al-Jilani in Baghdad. The source names two cities and two tombs: Ibn Arabi lies in the Salihiyya quarter of Damascus.
stops.campa: From Baghdad the pilgrimage goes on to Damascus, where on the slope of Mount Qasiyun the same eighteen-year-old prays at the grave of Ibn Arabi, the Andalusian who spent twelve days in Baghdad six centuries earlier without any source recording that he ever visited al-Jilani. The two tombs stand eight hundred kilometres apart and one pilgrim touches both inside a single season. He will die an old man a street's width from the Damascus stone and be buried beside it.
suggested_refs: The Ibn Arabi mosque and tomb at Salihiyya, Damascus

stops.name: Bab al-Sheikh, the Eleventh
stops.date_confidence: A continuing annual observance on 11 Rabi' al-Thani, with no first-attested date for the festival's origin in any source reachable this session; that origin is a gap. The date here is a placeholder for the present, not a claim about a year.
stops.campa: Every year on the eleventh of Rabi' al-Thani the day is kept as Gyarvi Sharif, the Eleventh, in Lahore and Kano and Konya and Linxia and here, under the dome Suleiman raised over the floor of the schoolroom. Nobody reachable can say when the observance started. What is dateable is the other end of it: a village on the Caspian shore, the first of Ramadan, four hundred and seventy years after the Hijra, a household that had no reason to expect any of this.
suggested_refs: Gyarvi Sharif, the annual observance of 11 Rabi' al-Thani at the Baghdad shrine and worldwide
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abdul Qadir Gilani' (which gives no origin date for the festival)
